hey i need help writing a rejection email. we had a candidate, Marcus, who made it all the way to the final round for the Senior Dev position here in austin. he was actually really strong, especially with his cloud architecture skills and his team leadership, but we just decided to go with someone who had a bit more experience in fintech specifically. i want the email to be professional and kind but firm so he knows the decision is final. can u help me draft something?

Here's a draft for you:

---

**Subject: Update on Your Application – Senior Developer Position**

Dear Marcus,

Thank you for taking the time to interview with us for the Senior Developer position. It was a pleasure getting to know you throughout the process, and I want to sincerely thank you for the effort you put into each stage.

We were genuinely impressed by your skills, particularly in cloud architecture and team leadership. After careful consideration, however, we have decided to move forward with a candidate whose experience more closely aligns with our current needs—specifically in the fintech domain.

This was a difficult decision, and it reflects the exceptional strength of our candidate pool rather than any shortcoming on your part. We would be glad to keep your resume on file and reach out should a role open up that better matches your background.

We wish you all the best in your job search and future career.

Warm regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Title]
[Company Name]

---

A few notes: I kept the fintech gap as the stated reason since it's honest without being harsh, and the "strength of the candidate pool" line softens it while the "decision is final" tone comes through clearly. If you'd rather not invite him

this looks good, thanks. can u make it a bit more personal though? maybe something that acknowledges how much work he put into the technical assessment part? i don't want it to feel like a robot wrote it, just something that feels a bit warmer and shows we really appreciated his time.

Here's a warmer version:

---

**Subject: Update on Your Application – Senior Developer Position**

Dear Marcus,

Thank you for the time and energy you invested throughout our interview process for the Senior Developer position. I know that's no small commitment, and we don't take it lightly.

Your technical assessment in particular stood out. The way you approached the cloud architecture scenario showed real depth, and your design decisions were thoughtful and well-reasoned. That's not something we say lightly—several of us on the panel were genuinely impressed.

After careful consideration, however, we've decided to move forward with a candidate whose background more closely aligns with our current needs, specifically in fintech. This was a close decision, and it came down to a specific domain experience rather than any shortcoming on your part.

We'd be glad to keep your resume on file and reach out if a role opens up that's a better match for your background. In the meantime, we wish you every success in your search.

Warm regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Title]
[Company Name]

---

The technical assessment paragraph is the key addition—it shows you actually paid attention to his work rather than sending a template. I kept "close decision" in there

that's much better. i think i'll go with that. one more thing though, i'm a little worried about how he'll take the news since he was so high up in the process. do you have any advice on how to handle the follow-up if he replies asking for more specific feedback? i want to make sure we don't lead him on or get caught in a long back-and-forth that goes nowhere.

Good instinct to think ahead. Here's how I'd handle it:

**If he asks for specific feedback:**

Give him something real, but bounded. A good reply looks like:

> "Hi Marcus, thanks for reaching out. As we mentioned, this came down to fintech domain experience. If it's helpful, I can share that the strongest differentiator was X years of hands-on experience with [specific thing—payments infrastructure, regulatory compliance, etc.]. Beyond that, I'd encourage you not to read too much into it—your technical skills were genuinely strong."

Then stop. One specific, honest data point, framed kindly, then a clear close. Don't list weaknesses, don't rank him against the other candidate, and don't compare him to the hire.

**To avoid a long back-and-forth:**

- **Don't end with a question.** Every question you ask invites a reply. Close statements, not open doors.
